case_info.scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

[Clinical case]
A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).

The specific pattern of shoulder hypertrophy, systemic symptoms, and bone marrow changes on MRI makes amyloid deposition the leading diagnosis, so initiating a workup for monoclonal gammopathy should be done concurrently, not deferred.

case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

case_info.scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.

     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

case_info.scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.
